questions.stem: Most of the water at Earth's surface is:
options: water vapour in the atmosphere
salt water in the oceans
fresh water in lakes and rivers
fresh water frozen in ice caps and glaciers
questions.explanation: About 97% of Earth's water is salt water in the oceans. Ice caps and glaciers hold most of the fresh water, but fresh water is only a small part of the total.

questions.stem: Why is only a small proportion of Earth's water available as drinking water?
options: Most fresh water has been made undrinkable by the natural acidity of rain
Most is chemically bound into rocks as minerals and cannot be released
Most is salty ocean water, and most fresh water is frozen or deep underground
Most is held in the atmosphere as vapour and cannot be collected as liquid
questions.explanation: Ocean water is too salty to drink without treatment, and of the small fraction that is fresh, most is locked in ice caps and glaciers or in groundwater that is hard to reach. Only a very small part of the atmosphere's mass is water vapour, and natural rain is only weakly acidic and safe to drink.

questions.stem: The boiling points of H₂S, H₂Se and H₂Te rise down group 16, yet water boils far higher than H₂S. Why?
options: Water molecules are linear, so they pack more closely than the bent H₂S molecules
Water molecules form hydrogen bonds, which are stronger than the forces between H₂S molecules
Water has the largest molar mass of the group 16 hydrides, so its dispersion forces are strongest
The O–H covalent bonds must be broken when water boils, but the H–S bonds do not break
questions.explanation: Oxygen is small and highly electronegative, so water forms hydrogen bonds; sulfur, selenium and tellurium do not. Water actually has the smallest molar mass of these hydrides, so dispersion forces cannot explain its high boiling point. No covalent bonds are broken on boiling, and both water and H₂S are bent.

questions.stem: What explains the rise in boiling point from H₂S to H₂Se to H₂Te?
options: Dispersion forces increase as the molecules get larger and have more electrons
Hydrogen bonding gets stronger as the central atom of the molecule gets larger
The covalent bonds between hydrogen and the central atom get stronger down the group
The molecules become more polar down the group, so dipole-dipole forces increase
questions.explanation: These molecules do not hydrogen bond, and their dipoles actually weaken down the group as electronegativity falls. What grows is the number of electrons, so dispersion forces strengthen and more energy is needed to separate the molecules. Covalent bonds are not broken when a molecular substance boils.

questions.stem: Why does ice float on liquid water?
options: The covalent bonds in ice are longer than the covalent bonds in liquid water
Hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open lattice with more space than in the liquid
Ice molecules have a smaller mass than the molecules in liquid water
Molecules in ice move faster than in the liquid, so they take up more space
questions.explanation: As water freezes, each molecule hydrogen bonds to four others in a regular, open arrangement that holds the molecules further apart than in the liquid. The same mass takes up more volume, so ice is less dense. Ice and water contain identical H₂O molecules, and molecules in a solid move less, not more.

questions.stem: In winter the surface of a pond freezes. Why can fish survive in the water underneath?
options: The ice forms on top and insulates the denser liquid water below it
Water is densest as a solid, so the ice sinks and the surface stays liquid
Ice has a high specific heat capacity, so it gives heat to the water below
Hydrogen bonds break as the water freezes, which warms the water beneath
questions.explanation: Because ice is less dense than liquid water, it forms a layer on the surface rather than sinking, and this layer slows the loss of heat from the water below. If ice sank, ponds would freeze from the bottom up. Freezing forms hydrogen bonds rather than breaking them.

questions.stem: Which value, with its units, is the specific heat capacity of liquid water?
options: 41.8 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹
4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹
4.18 kJ g⁻¹ °C⁻¹
questions.explanation: It takes 4.18 J of energy to raise the temperature of 1 g of water by 1 °C (the same as 1 K). 4.18 kJ is the energy for 1 kg, not 1 g, by 1 °C. The symbol for specific heat capacity is c, used in q = mcΔT.

questions.stem: How much energy is needed to heat 250 g of water from 20.0 °C to 80.0 °C?
questions.explanation: q = mcΔT = 250 × 4.18 × (80.0 − 20.0) = 62 700 J = 62.7 kJ. 83.6 kJ uses the final temperature instead of the change in temperature, and 15.0 kJ leaves out the specific heat capacity.

questions.stem: A 500 g sample of water absorbs 20.9 kJ of energy. By how much does its temperature rise?
questions.explanation: ΔT = q ÷ (mc) = 20 900 ÷ (500 × 4.18) = 10.0 °C. The energy must be in joules to match the units of c; leaving it as 20.9 gives 0.0100 °C.

questions.stem: Why does the high specific heat capacity of water help keep the temperature of coastal areas moderate?
options: Water reflects most of the sunlight that reaches it, so the sea stays cooler than the land
Water must absorb or release a lot of energy to change temperature, so the sea warms and cools slowly
Water molecules absorb the Sun's energy by breaking their covalent bonds, which stores the heat
Water has a low boiling point, so it evaporates quickly and cools the air above the coast
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonding means water needs a lot of energy for each degree of temperature change. The sea therefore heats up slowly in summer and cools slowly in winter, and nearby air follows it. Water's boiling point is high for its size, not low.

questions.stem: Water has a relatively high latent heat of vaporisation. What does this mean?
options: Very little energy is released when water vapour condenses back into a liquid
Water boils at a high temperature because its covalent bonds are very strong
A lot of energy is needed to turn liquid water into vapour without changing its temperature
A lot of energy is needed to raise the temperature of liquid water by one degree
questions.explanation: Latent heat of vaporisation is the energy needed to change liquid to gas at constant temperature, and for water it is high because hydrogen bonds must be overcome. Energy to raise the temperature describes specific heat capacity. The same large amount of energy is released when the vapour condenses.

questions.stem: How does water's high latent heat of vaporisation help regulate the temperature of the oceans and the life in them?
options: The energy absorbed in evaporation stays in the water left behind and raises its temperature
Evaporation breaks O–H bonds in surface water, so the Sun's energy is used up making gases
Evaporation removes a lot of energy from surface water, which limits how hot the ocean becomes
Evaporation adds energy to the surface water, which keeps the ocean warm through the night
questions.explanation: Molecules that evaporate carry away a large amount of energy, so evaporation cools the water that is left. Because each gram evaporated removes so much energy, the ocean surface cannot heat up quickly, which keeps conditions stable for aquatic life. Evaporation overcomes hydrogen bonds; it does not break O–H bonds.

questions.stem: According to the Bronsted–Lowry theory, an acid is a:
options: proton donor
proton acceptor
electron donor
hydroxide ion donor
questions.explanation: A Bronsted–Lowry acid donates a proton (H+ ion) to a base, which accepts it. Defining acids by hydroxide ions is the older Arrhenius idea for bases, and electron transfer describes redox reactions.

questions.stem: What is the conjugate base of HCO₃−?
options: CO₃2−
H₂CO₃
OH−
CO₂
questions.explanation: A conjugate base is what remains after an acid has donated a proton, so HCO₃− minus H+ gives CO₃2−. H₂CO₃ is the conjugate acid of HCO₃−, formed when it accepts a proton.

questions.stem: Which species is amphiprotic?
options: Cl−
HCO₃−
CO₃2−
NH₄+
questions.explanation: An amphiprotic species can both donate and accept a proton. HCO₃− can donate a proton to become CO₃2− or accept one to become H₂CO₃. CO₃2− can only accept a proton, NH₄+ can only donate one, and Cl− does not act as a base in water.

questions.stem: In the reaction HPO₄2−(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂PO₄−(aq) + OH−(aq), which statement is correct?
options: OH− is the conjugate acid of water in this reaction
H₂PO₄− is the conjugate base of HPO₄2− in this reaction
HPO₄2− acts as a base and water acts as an acid
HPO₄2− acts as an acid and water acts as a base
questions.explanation: HPO₄2− gains a proton to become H₂PO₄−, so it is the base, and water loses a proton to become OH−, so it is the acid. OH− is therefore water's conjugate base, and H₂PO₄− is the conjugate acid of HPO₄2−.

questions.stem: Phosphoric acid, H₃PO₄, is described as triprotic. What does this mean?
options: It contains three oxygen atoms that release H+
Each molecule can donate up to three protons
It ionises completely in three separate steps
Each molecule can accept up to three protons
questions.explanation: A polyprotic acid has more than one proton it can donate; phosphoric acid can lose three in turn, forming H₂PO₄−, HPO₄2− and PO₄3−. It is a weak acid, so none of the steps goes to completion. Accepting protons is the behaviour of a base.

questions.stem: Which equation shows ammonia acting as a Bronsted–Lowry base in water?
options: NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄+(aq) + OH−(aq)
NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₂−(aq) + H₃O+(aq)
NH₃(aq) + OH−(aq) ⇌ NH₄+(aq) + O2−(aq)
NH₃(aq) ⇌ N3−(aq) + 3H+(aq)
questions.explanation: As a base, ammonia accepts a proton from water to form NH₄+, leaving OH− and making the solution basic. Losing a proton to form NH₂− would be ammonia acting as an acid, which does not happen to any useful extent in water.

questions.stem: Ethanoic acid is described as a weak acid because it:
options: only partly ionises in water
is always found in dilute solutions
cannot react with reactive metals
forms solutions with a pH above 7
questions.explanation: Strength describes the extent of ionisation: in ethanoic acid solution only a small fraction of the molecules donate a proton to water. A weak acid can still be concentrated, and it still reacts with metals such as magnesium. Acid solutions have a pH below 7 at 25 °C.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a strong acid from a concentrated acid?
options: A strong acid is always concentrated, and a weak acid is always dilute
Strength and concentration both mean how low the pH of the solution is
Strength is how completely the acid ionises; concentration is how much acid is dissolved per litre
Strength is how much acid is dissolved per litre; concentration is how completely the acid ionises
questions.explanation: Strength is a property of the acid itself: hydrochloric acid ionises completely, ethanoic acid only partly. Concentration is the amount dissolved per litre and can be changed by adding water. So a dilute strong acid and a concentrated weak acid are both possible.

questions.stem: Hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid solutions, each 0.10 M, are compared at 25 °C. Which observation is expected?
options: Both have the same pH, because they have the same concentration
The ethanoic acid has a lower pH, because each molecule has more hydrogen atoms
Both conduct electricity equally well, because they have the same concentration
The hydrochloric acid has a lower pH and conducts electricity better
questions.explanation: Hydrochloric acid ionises completely, so its solution contains far more H₃O+ and other ions than ethanoic acid, which ionises only slightly. More H₃O+ means a lower pH, and more ions mean better conductivity. Only the hydrogen in ethanoic acid's –COOH group is acidic, so counting hydrogen atoms is misleading.

questions.stem: Which is the balanced full equation, with states, for hydrochloric acid reacting with calcium carbonate?
options: CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(s) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)
CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂CO₃(s)
CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)
CaCO₃(s) + HCl(aq) → CaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)
questions.explanation: An acid and a metal carbonate give a salt, water and carbon dioxide. Calcium forms Ca2+, so the salt is CaCl₂, which needs two HCl, and it stays dissolved as CaCl₂(aq). CaCl is not a real compound, and carbonic acid is not formed as a solid.

questions.stem: What is the ionic equation for the reaction between nitric acid and potassium hydroxide solutions?
options: H+(aq) + OH−(aq) → H₂O(l)
K+(aq) + NO₃−(aq) → KNO₃(s)
H+(aq) + NO₃−(aq) → HNO₃(l)
KOH(aq) → K+(aq) + OH−(aq)
questions.explanation: Both reactants are strong and fully ionised, and potassium nitrate is soluble, so K+ and NO₃− are spectator ions. Only H+ and OH− change, combining to form water. Potassium nitrate does not precipitate.

questions.stem: Sodium carbonate solution is added to hydrochloric acid. Which is the ionic equation for the reaction?
options: CO₃2−(aq) + 2H+(aq) → H₂CO₃(s)
2Na+(aq) + 2Cl−(aq) → 2NaCl(s)
CO₃2−(aq) + 2H+(aq) → H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)
CO₃2−(aq) + H+(aq) → H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)
questions.explanation: Na+ and Cl− are spectator ions because sodium chloride is soluble. Each carbonate ion takes two hydrogen ions to form water and carbon dioxide gas, which is the fizzing seen. With only one H+ the hydrogen and the charge do not balance.

questions.stem: Which compound is commonly used in antacids to neutralise excess stomach acid?
options: Ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH
Magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)₂
Sodium chloride, NaCl
Ammonium chloride, NH₄Cl
questions.explanation: Stomach acid is mainly hydrochloric acid, so an antacid must be a base. Magnesium hydroxide is only slightly soluble, so it neutralises the acid without making the stomach strongly basic; calcium carbonate and sodium hydrogen carbonate are also used. Ammonium chloride is slightly acidic, and sodium chloride is neutral.

questions.stem: Which equation, with states, shows magnesium hydroxide in an antacid neutralising stomach acid?
options: Mg(OH)₂(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(s) + 2H₂O(l)
Mg(OH)₂(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + 2H₂O(g)
Mg(OH)₂(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + 2H₂O(l)
Mg(OH)₂(s) + HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l)
questions.explanation: Each Mg(OH)₂ provides two hydroxide ions, so it needs two HCl and forms two water molecules. Magnesium chloride is soluble, so it is MgCl₂(aq), and the water forms as a liquid at body temperature. The equation with one HCl does not balance hydrogen, oxygen or chlorine.

questions.stem: How does the hydronium ion concentration of a solution with pH 3 compare with that of a solution with pH 5?
options: 2 times greater
100 times smaller
1000 times greater
100 times greater
questions.explanation: pH is a logarithmic scale: each unit lower is ten times more H₃O+. Two units lower means 10 × 10 = 100 times the concentration. A lower pH always means a higher hydronium concentration, so it cannot be smaller.

questions.stem: What is the pH of 0.010 M hydrochloric acid?
questions.explanation: HCl is a strong acid, so [H₃O+] = 0.010 M = 10⁻² M, and pH = −log₁₀(10⁻²) = 2.00. 12.00 would be the pH of a 0.010 M strong base.

questions.stem: What is the pH of 0.0010 M sodium hydroxide solution at 25 °C?
questions.explanation: [OH−] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ M, so [H₃O+] = Kw ÷ [OH−] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ ÷ 1.0 × 10⁻³ = 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ M, and pH = 11.00. 3.00 is the result of taking −log of the hydroxide concentration and stopping there.

questions.stem: What is the pH of 0.050 M barium hydroxide, Ba(OH)₂, at 25 °C?
questions.explanation: Each Ba(OH)₂ releases two OH− ions, so [OH−] = 0.10 M. Then [H₃O+] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ ÷ 0.10 = 1.0 × 10⁻¹³ M and pH = 13.00. Forgetting the factor of two gives 12.70.

questions.stem: At 50 °C the value of Kw is 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴. Which statement about pure water at 50 °C is correct?
options: Its pH is exactly 7, because it is neutral
Its pH is below 7, but it is still neutral
Its pH is above 7, so it is slightly basic
Its pH is below 7, so it is slightly acidic
questions.explanation: In pure water [H₃O+] = [OH−] = √(5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴) ≈ 2.3 × 10⁻⁷ M, giving a pH of about 6.6. Water is neutral whenever the two concentrations are equal, so a pH of 7 marks neutrality only at 25 °C.

questions.stem: Lemon juice has a pH of 2.4, blood 7.4, milk 6.6 and household ammonia 11.5. Which order runs from most acidic to most basic?
options: Ammonia, blood, milk, lemon juice
Lemon juice, blood, milk, ammonia
Milk, lemon juice, blood, ammonia
Lemon juice, milk, blood, ammonia
questions.explanation: The lower the pH, the more acidic the solution, so the order is 2.4, 6.6, 7.4, 11.5. Blood, at 7.4, is slightly basic, so it comes after milk, which is slightly acidic.

questions.stem: A pH meter gives readings of 4.12, 4.13 and 4.12 for a buffer solution whose true pH is 4.50. The readings are:
options: accurate but not precise
both accurate and precise
neither accurate nor precise
precise but not accurate
questions.explanation: The readings agree closely with each other, so they are precise, but they are all well away from the true value, so they are not accurate. This pattern suggests a systematic error, such as a meter that needs calibrating.

questions.stem: Why does a calibrated pH meter give a more accurate pH than an indicator made from red cabbage?
options: It measures the concentration of the acid rather than its pH
It gives a numerical reading close to the true value, not a colour judged by eye
It changes colour more sharply than any natural indicator can
It reacts with the acid and removes the hydronium ions it measures
questions.explanation: A natural indicator changes colour over a range of pH values, and the colour must be matched by eye, so it gives only an approximate pH. A calibrated meter reads the pH directly to one or two decimal places. A pH meter measures pH; it does not show colours or remove ions.

questions.stem: Unpolluted rain has a pH of about 5.6. What causes this natural acidity?
options: Nitrogen gas dissolves in rain, forming nitric acid, a strong acid
Oxygen gas dissolves in rain, forming a high concentration of H+
Carbon dioxide dissolves in rain, forming carbonic acid, a weak acid
Sulfur dioxide from power stations dissolves, forming sulfuric acid
questions.explanation: CO₂ in the air dissolves in rain water and reacts to form carbonic acid, H₂CO₃, which makes all rain slightly acidic. Acid rain, with a lower pH, comes from pollutants such as sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, so sulfuric acid from power stations is not natural acidity.

questions.stem: As more CO₂ dissolves in the oceans, why do marine invertebrates find it harder to build calcium carbonate shells?
options: The extra H+ reacts with carbonate ions, leaving fewer carbonate ions for shell building
The CO₂ reacts with the calcium ions in seawater to form insoluble calcium oxide
The seawater becomes more basic, and calcium carbonate dissolves in basic solutions
The CO₂ forms a strong acid that ionises completely and removes the calcium ions
questions.explanation: Dissolved CO₂ forms carbonic acid, which donates H+. These hydrogen ions react with CO₃2− to form HCO₃−, so less carbonate is available for animals to combine with Ca2+ to make CaCO₃. The ocean becomes less basic, not more, and carbonic acid is a weak acid.

questions.stem: In a redox reaction, the oxidising agent is the species that:
options: loses electrons and is itself oxidised
gains electrons and is itself oxidised
donates protons to the other reactant
gains electrons and is itself reduced
questions.explanation: An oxidising agent causes another species to be oxidised by taking electrons from it, so the oxidising agent gains electrons and is reduced. Losing electrons and being oxidised describes the reducing agent. Proton transfer is an acid-base reaction, not redox.

questions.stem: In the reaction Zn(s) + Cu2+(aq) → Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s), which species is the reducing agent?
options: Cu(s)
Zn(s)
Cu2+(aq)
Zn2+(aq)
questions.explanation: Zinc atoms lose two electrons each to form Zn2+, so zinc is oxidised, and in doing so it reduces Cu2+ to copper. The species that is oxidised is the reducing agent. Cu2+ gains electrons, so it is the oxidising agent.

questions.stem: When iron rusts, which half-equation shows the oxidation of the iron?
options: Fe2+(aq) + 2e− → Fe(s)
Fe(s) + 2e− → Fe2+(aq)
O₂(g) + 2H₂O(l) + 4e− → 4OH−(aq)
Fe(s) → Fe2+(aq) + 2e−
questions.explanation: Oxidation is loss of electrons, so the electrons appear on the product side as iron atoms become Fe2+ ions. The oxygen half-equation is the reduction that happens at the same time. Adding electrons to iron and getting a positive ion does not balance the charge.

questions.stem: Which is the balanced half-equation for the reduction of MnO₄− to Mn2+ in acidic conditions?
options: MnO₄−(aq) + 4H+(aq) + 5e− → Mn2+(aq) + 2H₂O(l)
MnO₄−(aq) + 8H+(aq) + 3e− → Mn2+(aq) + 4H₂O(l)
MnO₄−(aq) + 8H+(aq) → Mn2+(aq) + 4H₂O(l) + 5e−
MnO₄−(aq) + 8H+(aq) + 5e− → Mn2+(aq) + 4H₂O(l)
questions.explanation: Balance oxygen with four H₂O, then hydrogen with eight H+, then charge: the left has −1 + 8 = +7 and the right has +2, so five electrons are added to the left. With only 4H+ and 2H₂O the oxygen does not balance, and electrons on the product side would make this an oxidation.

questions.stem: The half-equations Fe2+(aq) → Fe3+(aq) + e− and MnO₄−(aq) + 8H+(aq) + 5e− → Mn2+(aq) + 4H₂O(l) are combined. How many Fe2+ ions react with each MnO₄− ion?
questions.explanation: Electrons lost must equal electrons gained. Each MnO₄− gains five electrons and each Fe2+ loses one, so the iron half-equation is multiplied by five: 5Fe2+ + MnO₄− + 8H+ → 5Fe3+ + Mn2+ + 4H₂O. The 8 is the number of hydrogen ions, not iron ions.

questions.stem: A strip of copper is placed in silver nitrate solution. What happens?
options: Copper forms on the strip and the solution turns colourless as Ag+ ions form
Nothing is seen, because copper is less reactive than silver and cannot react
Silver forms on the copper and bubbles of hydrogen are given off from the strip
Silver forms on the copper and the solution turns blue as Cu2+ ions form
questions.explanation: Copper is above silver in the reactivity series, so it is oxidised to blue Cu2+ ions and reduces Ag+ to silver metal: Cu(s) + 2Ag+(aq) → Cu2+(aq) + 2Ag(s). Copper is more reactive than silver, not less, and no hydrogen is produced because no acid is involved.

questions.stem: Which metal will displace iron from iron(II) sulfate solution?
options: Lead
Zinc
Copper
Silver
questions.explanation: A metal displaces another from solution only if it is higher in the reactivity series. Zinc is above iron, so it is oxidised to Zn2+ while Fe2+ is reduced to iron. Copper, silver and lead are all below iron.

questions.stem: Iron objects corrode faster in sea water than in fresh water. Why?
options: Sea water contains no dissolved oxygen, and oxygen is what protects iron from rusting
Chloride ions donate electrons to the iron atoms, turning them into iron(II) ions
The dissolved ions make sea water a better electrolyte, speeding up electron transfer
Sodium ions in the sea water are strong oxidising agents that react directly with iron
questions.explanation: Rusting is a redox process in which iron is oxidised and oxygen is reduced, with ions moving through the water between the sites. The high concentration of dissolved ions in sea water makes this transfer faster. Sodium ions are very weak oxidising agents, and oxygen is a reactant in rusting rather than a protection.

questions.stem: A simple primary cell is made with zinc and copper electrodes in an electrolyte. Which electrode is oxidised?
options: Copper, because it is the more reactive metal
Copper, because it is the less reactive metal
Zinc, because it is the less reactive metal
Zinc, because it is the more reactive metal
questions.explanation: In a primary cell the more reactive metal is the stronger reducing agent, so zinc loses electrons and is oxidised. The electrons flow through the external circuit to the copper electrode, where reduction occurs. Copper is below zinc in the reactivity series.
